1.o: In this chapter we have a twofold comparison stated: I. Between the evangelical and legal dispensation; and the excellency of the gospel above that of the law is asserted and proved, ver. 1-3. II. Between the glory of Christ and that of the highest creatures, the angels; where the pre-eminence is justly given to the Lord Jesus Christ, and clearly demonstrated to belong to him, ver. 4, to the end.
1.i: Hebrews 1 and 2 introduce Jesus as God's final word, greater than the prophets and angels, and a brother who shares our life.
1.p: Lord Jesus, thank You for sharing our life. Keep us from drifting, and help us in every test. Amen.
1.l: Tie one thing down today that tends to drift, a plan or a promise, and write it where you will see it.
q: Hebrews says Jesus shared flesh and blood so He could help us when we are tested. What helps you most when you are tested?

2.o: In this chapter the apostle, I. Makes some application of the doctrine laid down in the chapter foregoing concerning the excellency of the person of Christ, both by way of exhortation and argument, ver. 1-4. II. Enlarges further upon the pre-eminence of Christ above the angels, ver. 5-9. III. Proceeds to remove the scandal of the cross, ver. 10-15. IV. Asserts the incarnation of Christ, taking upon him not the nature of angels, but the seed of Abraham, and assigns the reason of his so doing, ver. 16, to the end.
2.i: Hebrews 1 and 2 introduce Jesus as God's final word, greater than the prophets and angels, and a brother who shares our life.
2.p: Lord Jesus, thank You for sharing our life. Keep us from drifting, and help us in every test. Amen.
2.l: Tie one thing down today that tends to drift, a plan or a promise, and write it where you will see it.
q: Hebrews says Jesus shared flesh and blood so He could help us when we are tested. What helps you most when you are tested?

3.o: In this chapter the apostle applies what he had said in the chapter foregoing concerning the priesthood of Christ, I. In a serious pathetic exhortation that this great high priest, who was discovered to them, might be seriously considered by them, ver. 1-6. II. He then adds many weighty counsels and cautions, ver. 7, to the end.
3.s: Rest and the Throne of Grace
3.i: Hebrews 3 and 4 move from Moses to rest, and end with one of the best-loved invitations in the Bible.
3.p: Lord Jesus, You were tested as we are. Help us come to Your throne with courage, and find mercy and grace when we need it. Amen.
3.l: Today, when you notice you are about to say no to something good, stop and ask if you are hardening your heart.
q: The writer says Jesus was tested in every way and did not sin. What does it mean to you that He understands?

4.o: The apostle, having in the foregoing chapter set forth the sin and punishment of the ancient Jews, proceeds in this, I. To declare that our privileges by Christ under the gospel exceed the privileges of the Jewish church under Moses, as a reason why we should make a right improvement of them, ver. 1-4. II. He assigns the cause why the ancient Hebrews did not profit by their religious privileges, ver. 2. Then, III. Confirms the privileges of those who believe, and the misery of those who continue in unbelief, ver.
4.s: Rest and the Throne of Grace
4.i: Hebrews 3 and 4 move from Moses to rest, and end with one of the best-loved invitations in the Bible.
4.p: Lord Jesus, You were tested as we are. Help us come to Your throne with courage, and find mercy and grace when we need it. Amen.

5.o: In this chapter the apostle continues his discourse upon the priesthood of Christ, a sweet subject, which he would not too soon dismiss. And here, I. He explains the nature of the priestly office in general, ver. 1-3. II. The proper and regular call there must be to this office, ver. 4-6. III. The requisite qualifications for the work, ver. 7-9. IV. The peculiar order of the priesthood of Christ; it was not after the order of Aaron, but of Melchisedec, ver. 6, 7, 10. V.
5.i: Hebrews 5 to 7 compare Jesus with the priests of Israel, and reach back to a mysterious king who met Abraham.
5.p: Lord Jesus, our priest forever, thank You that You always speak for us. Help us to grow up in You. Amen.
5.l: Try something a little harder than usual to learn today, and finish it, as a way of eating solid food.
q: The writer says some readers needed milk instead of solid food. What is a hard idea you are ready to chew on?

6.o: In this chapter the apostle proceeds to persuade the Hebrews to make a better proficiency in religion than they had done, as the best way to prevent apostasy, the dreadful nature and consequences of which sin he sets forth in a serious manner (ver. 1-8), and then expresses his good hopes concerning them, that they would persevere in faith and holiness, to which he exhorts them, and sets before them the great encouragement they had from God, both with respect to their duty and happiness, ver. 9, to the end.
6.i: Hebrews 5 to 7 compare Jesus with the priests of Israel, and reach back to a mysterious king who met Abraham.
6.p: Lord Jesus, our priest forever, thank You that You always speak for us. Help us to grow up in You. Amen.
6.l: Try something a little harder than usual to learn today, and finish it, as a way of eating solid food.
q: The writer says some readers needed milk instead of solid food. What is a hard idea you are ready to chew on?

7.o: The doctrine of the priestly office of Christ is so excellent in itself, and so essential a part of the Christian faith, that the apostle loves to dwell upon it. Nothing made the Jews so fond of the Levitical dispensation as the high esteem they had of their priesthood, and it was doubtless a sacred and most excellent institution; it was a very severe threatening denounced against the Jews (Hos. iii.

7.p: Lord Jesus, our priest forever, thank You that You always speak for us. Help us to grow up in You. Amen.

8.o: In this chapter the apostle pursues his former subject, the priesthood of Christ. And, I. He sums up what he had already said, ver. 1, 2. II. He sets before them the necessary parts of the priestly office, ver. 3-5. And, III. Largely illustrates the excellency of the priesthood of Christ, by considering the excellency of that new dispensation or covenant for which Christ is the Mediator, ver. 6, to the end.
8.i: Hebrews 8 to 10 explain why Jesus' one sacrifice replaced the old tent and its offerings.
8.p: Lord, thank You for the sacrifice that was enough. Write Your law on our hearts, and let us come near with a true heart. Amen.
8.l: Write down one promise from today's reading on a card, and put it where you will see it.
q: A covenant meant 'a cutting.' What promise in your life was costly enough to be cut into you?

9.o: The apostle, having declared the Old-Testament dispensation antiquated and vanishing away, proceeds to let the Hebrews see the correspondence there was between the Old Testament and the New; and that whatever was excellent in the Old was typical and representative of the New, which therefore must as far excel the Old as the substance does the shadow. The Old Testament was never intended to be rested in, but to prepare for the institutions of the gospel. And here he treats, I.
9.i: Hebrews 8 to 10 explain why Jesus' one sacrifice replaced the old tent and its offerings.
9.p: Lord, thank You for the sacrifice that was enough. Write Your law on our hearts, and let us come near with a true heart. Amen.
9.l: Write down one promise from today's reading on a card, and put it where you will see it.
q: A covenant meant 'a cutting.' What promise in your life was costly enough to be cut into you?

10.o: The apostle knew very well that the Hebrews, to whom he wrote, were strangely fond of the Levitical dispensation, and therefore he fills his mouth with arguments to wean them from it; and in order thereto proceeds in this chapter, I. To lay low the whole of that priesthood and sacrifice, ver. 1-6. II. He raises and exalts the priesthood of Christ very high, that he might effectually recommend him and his gospel to them, ver. 7-18. III.
10.i: Hebrews 8 to 10 explain why Jesus' one sacrifice replaced the old tent and its offerings.
10.p: Lord, thank You for the sacrifice that was enough. Write Your law on our hearts, and let us come near with a true heart. Amen.
10.l: Write down one promise from today's reading on a card, and put it where you will see it.
q: A covenant meant 'a cutting.' What promise in your life was costly enough to be cut into you?

11.o: The apostle having, in the close of the foregoing chapter, recommended the grace of faith and a life of faith as the best preservative against apostasy, he how enlarges upon the nature and fruits of this excellent grace. I. The nature of it, and the honour it reflects upon all who live in the exercise of it, ver. 1-3. II. The great examples we have in the Old Testament of those who lived by faith, and died and suffered extraordinary things by the strength of his grace, ver. 4-38. And, III.
11.i: Hebrews 11 tells how Abel, Noah, Abraham, and Sarah lived by faith, trusting God's promises they did not see fulfilled.
11.p: Lord, give us faith like Abraham's, to follow You when we cannot see the end. Amen.
11.l: Do one small thing today because you trust God, even though you can't see how it will turn out.
q: What unseen thing do you act on every day?

12.o: The apostle, in this chapter, applies what he has collected in the chapter foregoing, and makes use of it as a great motive to patience and perseverance in the Christian faith and state, pressing home the argument, I. From a greater example than he had yet mentioned, and that is Christ himself, ver. 1-3. II. From the gentle and gracious nature of the afflictions they endured in their Christian course, ver. 4-17. III.
12.i: Hebrews 12 and 13 finish the letter with a race, a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and a list of plain, kind commands.
12.p: Lord Jesus, author and finisher of our faith, help us run with patience, and make us kind to strangers. Amen.
12.l: Welcome someone new this week, at school, church or home, and make them feel they belong.
q: The writer says some have welcomed angels without knowing it. Who might you be welcoming without knowing?

13.o: The apostle, having treated largely of Christ, and faith, and free grace, and gospel privileges, and warned the Hebrews against apostasy, now, in the close of all, recommends several excellent duties to them, as the proper fruits of faith (ver. 1-17); he then bespeaks their prayers for him, and offers up his prayers to God for them, gives them some hope of seeing himself and Timothy, and ends with the general salutation and benediction, ver. 18, to the end.
13.i: Hebrews 12 and 13 finish the letter with a race, a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and a list of plain, kind commands.
13.p: Lord Jesus, author and finisher of our faith, help us run with patience, and make us kind to strangers. Amen.
